title: Phase 2: ASP.NET Core API and React application
description: Scaffold the ASP.NET Core minimal API and React 19 application shells. Establish the vertical-slice folder layout, configure dependency injection, and wire up the first end-to-end flow for submitting an expense report.

data.text: In this phase you'll stand up the application shells. The API and React app will evolve together, but the API must be usable independently — never let the React component dictate backend structure.
Vertical slice vs. layered folder structure

For the Application layer, we prefer vertical slices over the traditional feature-less Service/Repository separation. Each feature (e.g., SubmitExpenseReport) owns its handler, validator, DTOs, and mapper in one folder. This keeps related changes together during code reviews and reduces the blast radius of refactors.

data.title: Vertical slice structure
items: Expense.Application/Shared/ → cross-cutting concerns like IPipelineBehavior, Result<T>.

data.title: Program.cs: minimal API with vertical slice registration
data.content: Keep Program.cs focused on composition. Handlers should not be added here one-by-one — use Scrutor or reflection.

data.text: The submit flow is the heart of the platform. It accepts a list of line items with optional receipt metadata, validates against policy, and returns a report ID with validation errors if any.

data.title: C#: SubmitExpenseReportCommand DTO
data.content: DTOs are records for immutability. Domain-specific types (Money, LineItemCategory) prevent invalid input at compile time.

data.title: C#: SubmitExpenseReportHandler
data.content: Handlers are thin orchestration layers. They map input, call domain methods, persist via unit of work, and return a Result<T>.

data.text: The React app is a Vite + TypeScript + React 19 project. Feature-based folder structure mirrors the backend vertical slices.

data.title: React folder structure
items: src/features/expense-reports/ → components, hooks, api.ts, types.ts, pages.
src/features/auth/ → login, session management, role guards.
src/lib/ → axios instance with auth interceptor, react-query hooks, error mapping.

data.title: TypeScript: expense report submit API client
data.content: The API client returns typed responses and maps backend errors to user-friendly messages. Never expose raw ProblemDetails to the UI.

data.title: Avoid leaking backend shapes to the frontend
data.text: Map DTOs to presentation models in the API layer or a dedicated shared-types package. If you return EF Core navigation properties in a JSON response, you've leaked your persistence model to every consumer.

data.title: React: NewExpenseReport form component
data.content: The form collects line items and submits. Validation errors from the backend are surfaced inline.

items.text: ASP.NET Core API solution with 5 projects (Domain, Application, Infrastructure, Api, Shared).
First MediatR handler (SubmitExpenseReport) end-to-end wired with DI.
React 19 + Vite app scaffolded with Vite proxy to API.
axios client with auth interceptor and typed error mapping.
NewExpenseReport form with dynamic line items and submit mutation.
OpenAPI/Swagger available at /swagger for API exploration.

data.title: Phase 2 summary
points: Vertical slices keep handlers, validators, and DTOs co-located per use case.
MediatR + ValidationBehavior keeps controllers thin and controllers testable.
React mirrors the backend slices under features/ for parity.
API contract is the boundary: never return EF entities directly.
data.takeaway: You now have a running shell. The next phases add the security, data, and resilience layers — but the skeleton is stable enough to build on.
